data: The suit worn on Apollo 11–14 — the first to support EVA on another world

First operational lunar surface suit. Hard upper torso, soft-fabric arms and legs, integrated lunar overboots, PLSS backpack with sublimator cooling and LiOH CO₂ scrubber, OPS emergency O₂ cylinder above the PLSS. Operating pressure 3.7 psi pure O₂ — lowest of any flown suit, to maximise mobility for walking in 1/6 g.
The first operational lunar surface suit — Apollo 11 through 14

A pressure suit on the Moon is really a spacecraft you wear — the smallest crewed vehicle Apollo built, sized for one. The A7L had to do everything a capsule does — hold pressure, supply oxygen, carry away heat and exhaled carbon dioxide, shield against a temperature swing of hundreds of degrees between sunlight and shadow — while still letting a person kneel, walk, and pick up a rock. Those two demands fight each other, because anything holding pressure wants to go stiff as a balloon. Its answer was twenty-one layers built around a rubber-coated bladder, with the backpack making the whole thing self-contained for hours. It was the first suit rated to walk on another world, and for its missions it was the only thing between a human being and vacuum.

First operational lunar surface suit. Hard upper torso, soft-fabric arms and legs, integrated lunar overboots, PLSS backpack with sublimator cooling and LiOH CO₂ scrubber, OPS emergency O₂ cylinder above the PLSS. Operating pressure 3.7 psi pure O₂ — lowest of any flown suit, to maximise mobility for walking in 1/6 g. Flew on Apollo 11 (the first Moonwalk), Apollo 12, and Apollo 13–14. Worn by Buzz Aldrin in the iconic gold-visor lunar surface photo.
